Vol.:(0123456789)

AI raises concerns over exacerbating data-driven deci- sion biases (Wang, 2021) and enabling academic cheating through generative AI (Chung Kwan, [2023)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). In this context, the teacher plays a key role in facilitating students’ effective and appropriate use of AI, as well as interacting with AI. In line with this, teachers need technological pedagogical and content knowledge (TPACK) to enhance students to use AI (Kim et al., 2022).

TPACK is a widely used teacher knowledge model to understand teaching with technology (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Numerous studies have developed scales to examine teachers’ TPACK knowledge in a variety of contexts (Baser et al., [2016;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Chai et al., [2020;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Schmidt et al., 2009). As more AI technologies emerge, teachers face challenges in constructing AI-supported teaching practices with appro- priate AI tools (Ng et al., 2023). Consequently, the integra- tion of AI into educational settings has sparked a surge of interest among researchers in developing AI-related TPACK within the teaching domain (An et al., [2023a;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Celik, [2023)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). However, unlike traditional information technology, AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems and chatbots can inde- pendently assume the role of teachers to promote learning from cognitive and content perspectives (Jiang, 2022). The particular attribute has not been previously explored in exist- ing research on AI and TPACK.

Most importantly for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, AI has introduced an authentic learning environment that allows EFL learners to interact with a functionally fluent interlocutor (Ji et al., 2023). Today, a rich variety of AI functions are available in EFL learning, such as chatbots, speech recognition, automatic writing correction, and adaptive recommendation of vocabulary and reading materials (An et al., [2023b)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). It is evident that teachers need to understand both the pedagogical advan- tages and pitfalls of using AI to effectively support stu- dents’ learning. However, few studies have focused on teachers’ perceptions of how AI can act as assistant teacher in supporting EFL students’ learning based on TPACK, and the limited research available has inadequately high- lighted the differences between AI and previous non-intel- ligent technologies ones (An et al., [2023a;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Celik, [2023)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design), particularly its capability as an autonomous machine teacher. Existing AI technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK) scales often adapt conventional TPACK scales by simply replacing other technologies with AI, without emphasizing AI’s distinctive attributes (An et al., [2023a;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Celik, [2023;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Ning et al., 2024). Besides, the current AI-related TPACK scales still suffer from issues prevalent in earlier TPACK scales, such as unclear sub- ject specificity, lack of a concrete application context, and ambiguous wording (Koehler & Mishra, 2016). Therefore, this study aimed to extend TPACK by developing a pre- cise, subject-specific, and contextually grounded scale to

measure EFL teachers’ AI-related TPACK based on the duo-agent notion to help teacher developers to identify teachers’ TPACK gaps.

## Literature Review

### Teachers’ Use of Educational AI

The use of AI in education has given rise to a new inter- disciplinary field known as AIED (Artificial Intelligence in Education) (Hwang et al., [2020)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). AIED has transformed the role of teachers, necessitating a redefinition of their respon- sibilities and competencies (An et al., [2023a)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design), but teach- ers’ AI knowledge and skills remain below expected levels (Dogan et al., [2025)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). Teachers are expected to collaborate with AI tools, which can autonomously perform tasks such as providing real-time feedback, adaptive assessments, and personalized recommendations (Hwang et al., [2020)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). Moreover, with advanced intelligence, AI can offer learners personalized instruction, effectively serving as a machine alternative to human teachers in various learning scenarios (Jiang, 2022). To leverage these AI tools effectively, human teachers must understand their capabilities and limitations (Xu & Ouyang, 2022), and discern where to replace or aug- ment teaching tasks. This enables the design of new human- AI duo-agent teaching that exploits AI’s independent peda- gogical strengths while refining teaching practices. Despite the benefits of AIED, researchers have acknowl- edged that the application of AI does not guarantee posi- tive learning outcomes (Xu & Ouyang, 2022). Studies have shown teacher support is important for learners’ learning with AI (Chiu et al., [2023)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). AIED may fall short in areas such as accurate and nuanced scoring for students’ artifacts and providing emotional support for students (Kang et al., 2023). Feedback from human teachers was more detailed, multifaceted, and emotionally supportive, highlighting the complementary roles of human and AI in education (Gao, [2021)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). Moreover, while AI excels at defined tasks, it strug- gles with complex contexts, underscoring teachers’ criti- cal role. Therefore, it is imperative to study how teachers can effectively integrate AI into their practices, not only to maximize the benefits of AI but also to ensure pedagogically sound and technologically advanced educational designs. Researchers have called for an AI-related TPACK model to support teachers in acquiring the knowledge needed to integrate AI into teaching practices (Crompton et al., [2022)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). However, the existing model did not seem to fully explicate the teaching roles of machine and hence may lack specificity, requiring further exploration.

Development of an Artificial Intelligence Technology Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI‑TPACK)…

### Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge

Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), proposed by Shul- man (1986), is a fundamental framework in teacher devel- opment. This framework integrates two core domains, con- tent knowledge (CK) and pedagogical knowledge (PK). CK means subject-specific expertise (what to teach), and PK means general instructional methods and learning theories (how to teach). PCK integrates CK and PK into a unified professional knowledge framework, establishing teaching as a uniquely integrative practice. Based on the PCK theory, Mishra and Koehler (2006) extended the theory by incorpo- rating technological knowledge, thereby proposing techno- logical pedagogical and content knowledge (TPACK). Seven dimensions of the TPACK model are delineated, including PK, CK, PCK, technological knowledge (TK), technologi- cal pedagogical knowledge (TPK), technological content knowledge (TCK), and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPCK) (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Building upon the TPACK framework, numerous schol- ars have adapted and applied TPACK across various con- texts including academic disciplines (e.g., EFL, Baser et al., [2016)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design), and diverse technological environments (e.g., interactive whiteboards, Jang & Tsai, [2012;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Internet tech- nologies, Zhou et al., 2017; educational robotics, Yanis & Yuruk, 2020). Most recently, the TPACK framework has been adapted for AI technologies (An et al., [2023a;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Celik, [2023;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Ning et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025) using self-report scale. Existing AI-TPACK scales inadequately address AI’s unique features and retain TPACK limitations like unclear subject specificity (Koehler & Mishra, 2016; Hava & Babayiğit, [2025)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design), contextual gaps (Celik, [2023;](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) Ning et al., 2024), and ambiguous terminology (Ng et al., 2023), hindering accurate assessment of teachers’ AI-integration capabilities. Refinements are needed to enhance validity and contextual relevance.

### AI in EFL Teaching

As previously mentioned, many AI products have been suc- cessfully integrated into EFL teaching, showcasing distinct functionalities that enable them to either independently guide student learning or assist human teachers. On the one hand, some AI systems can autonomously assume roles traditionally held by human teachers. For example, AI can assume teachers’ responsibilities in automated essay grad- ing, thereby enabling teachers to reallocate time toward higher-order instructional tasks (Wang & Han, 2022). Fur- thermore, AI chatbots can create immersive dialog prac- tice environments to enhance students’ communicative motivation (Tai & Chen, 2023). On the other hand, there are AI tools designed to assist human teachers rather than replace them. AI can help EFL teachers collect and analyze 

multidimensional data, enabling them to provide targeted instruction (Kim, 2023). By leveraging these complementary roles, AI and human teachers can work together to create a more effective and personalized learning experience. Meanwhile, AI in EFL teaching also has limitations, such as mechanical language and lack of the natural body lan- guage and facial expressions, emphasizing the irreplaceable role of human teachers. Human teachers can leverage their intelligence and creativity to address areas where AI falls short, providing nuanced emotional support (Jia & Cheng, 2024) and useful learning strategies in AI-supported EFL (Sun & Yang, 2023). Furthermore, teachers can utilize AI to collect and analyze multidimensional data, enabling them to provide targeted instruction and feedback tailored to indi- vidual student needs (Kim, 2023). Therefore, EFL teach- ers need to understand the teaching capabilities of AI and know how to leverage their own instructional design skills to collaborate with AI to achieve a new level of pedagogical human–machine coupling that empowers students’ learning. While prior studies confirm AI’s efficacy in specific teaching tasks, critical gaps persist in AI-supported EFL teaching research. First, the conceptual frameworks defining teachers’ specialized knowledge for human-AI collaboration are absent, which is arguably an important conceptual unit to facilitate teachers’ development and integration of AI. Second, due to this measurement deficit, the current pro- ficiency levels of EFL teachers in AI integration may not be comprehensively assessed. This may hinder evidence- based policymaking and sustainable development of AI- augmented language pedagogy. Hence, there is a need to construct and validate assessment tools to quantify teachers- AI collaboration.

## Research Model and Research Questions

As already mentioned, human teachers need to first com- prehend the capability possessed by AI as a teacher. Chief among these capabilities is instructional expertise. This understanding is crucial for fostering effective collabora- tion between human and AI in EFL. Therefore, AI-TPK is divided into two parts, AI-TPK (machine teacher) and AI- TPK (human teacher). EFL teachers need first to possess AI-TPK (machine teacher), which entails understanding the pedagogical knowledge possessed by machine teach- ers. Besides, EFL teachers need to possess AI-TPK (human teacher), which means that they need to know how to inte- grate AI with human pedagogy to maximize efficiency, capi- talize on AI’s strengths, and surpass its shortcomings. Based on this division of AI-TPK, AI-TPCK can also be catego- rized into two parts: AI-TPCK (machine teacher) and AI- TPCK (human teacher). So, we proposed a new AI-TPACK model (see Fig. [1)](#creating-valid-measurement-is-foundational-to-the-verifi--cation-of-concepts-and-the-use-of-concepts-for-improvement).

accordingly. The definitions of AI-TPACK and the final item count are presented in Table [1.](#creating-valid-measurement-is-foundational-to-the-verifi--cation-of-concepts-and-the-use-of-concepts-for-improvement)

Initially, an item pool comprising 56 draft items was developed based on literature review. The items were then reviewed by an expert in the field of AI and three experts in the field of educational technology who had expertise in TPACK scale development and AI. They evaluated items in terms of their clarity, accuracy, and content relevance to establish their content and face validity. Based on their suggestions, we avoided the use of specific technical terms while clearly articulating the functionality of the technolo- gies, and removed some items. For example, the item “I know that AI requires massive data for machine learning” which has little to do with applying AI, was removed. As a result, the instrument was reduced to 24 items comprising six dimensions.

Emulating Archambault and Crippen’s ([2009)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) proce- dures, we also employed a think-aloud strategy to ensure construct validity. Think-aloud participants were three EFL teachers. After a brief introduction of each dimension, they were asked to explain what they were thinking when brows- ing each question and to consider whether the item fit the dimension. Based on the feedback received, several items were modified to ensure clarity and better alignment with reality. For instance, the item “I know that AI-based tools can provide scoring and feedback on English compositions for students” was changed based on teachers’ perception that current AI technology tools can only provide feedback on grammar errors. Therefore, it was revised to “I know that AI-based tools can give students feedback on grammatical errors in English composition” to ensure that each item cor- responded to a real-life EFL teaching scenario. The options used a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

To establish criterion-related validity, we employed Performance Expectancy (PE), Effort Expectancy (EE), and Behavioral Intention (BI) items of the AI technology acceptance scale developed by An et al. ([2023a)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). This instrument has undergone comprehensive psychomet- ric validation, demonstrating robust reliability (Cronbach’s α \> 0.7 across scales) and good validity (favorable explora- tory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis results) 

### Participants and Data Collection

The study recruited in-service secondary school EFL teach- ers involved in a teacher development project called “Inte- gration of AI and English Teaching” in the Chinese Smart Education Demonstration Zone. These teachers had access to various AI tools for EFL teaching and learning and par- ticipated in over a year of action research to explore their effective use, supported by AI companies and expert con- sortia. Professional development courses were also provided to enhance their AI-TPACK. A total of 285 questionnaires were collected, and 243 valid samples were retained for scale test, with participant demographics detailed in Table [2.](#participants-anddata-collection) The proportion of male teachers is 3.29%, which is in line with the current distribution of Chinese EFL teachers.

### Data Analysis

A normality test and a quality test of each item were con- ducted first. The normality was tested using skewness (abso- lute value of skewness \< 1) and kurtosis (absolute value of kurtosis \< 2) values (Noar, 2003). Item quality was assessed via t-tests comparing the differences between top 27% and bottom 27% of scores. Items with t-values above 3.0 were deemed acceptable and retained.

The construct validity of the instrument was analyzed through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). According to the guideline offered by Hair et al. ([2014)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design), the evaluation criteria of fit indices are as follows: the chi-squared (χ2)/ degrees of freedom (_df_) ≤ 3.0, the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) \< 0.1, Comparative Fit Index (CFI) \> 0.9 and the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) \> 0.9. To test convergent validity, factor loadings and average variance extracted (AVE) were examined. If the absolute values of factor loadings are greater than 0.5 and AVE is at least 0.5, it is acceptable for practical significance (Hair et al., [2014)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). To check discriminant validity, we employed the average vari- ance extracted method. If the square root value of AVEs of dimensions is higher than the correlation coefficient between dimensions, the discrimination validity is good (Fornell &

To check reliability, the Cronbach’s alpha (α) coefficient and composite reliability (CR) were com- puted, both of which should be more than 0.7 to testify to the reliability of the construct (Hair et al., [2014)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). To test criterion-related validity, we conducted correlation analyses between the target construct (AI-TPACK) and theoretically aligned criterion measures (AI technology acceptance). Pearson correlation coefficients (r) should exceed 0.40 to demonstrate moderate practical significance (Noar, 2003). Finally, descriptive statistics were employed to gain an understanding of the overall status of EFL teachers on AI- TPACK. Independent sample t-tests examined differences based on educational level, while an analysis of variance (ANOVA) explored differences among age groups. Mplus8.0 (for CFA), Microsoft Excel 2019 (for calculating the square root of AVEs) and SPSS 20.0 (for other data calculations) were utilized to process the collected data.

### Item Analysis

First of all, the skewness and kurtosis values of each item were calculated; the results are presented in Table [3.](#result) The

### Validity and Reliability Analysis

In the initial CFA analysis, the χ2/_df_ was 3.11 (\> 3.0), the RMSEA was 0.093 (\< 0.1), the CFI was 0.911 (\> 0.9), and the TLI was 0.895 (≯ 0.9). According to Hair et al. ([2014)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design), the revision of the model was carried out. Based on modifi- cation indices, one item was excluded from the AI-TCK con- struct due to its low factor loading (λ \< 0.5, see Appendix 1). After the modifications, the revised model showed improved fit: χ2/_df_ = 3.001 (≈ 3), RMSEA = 0.091 (\< 0.1), CFI = 0.916 (\> 0.9), and TLI = 0.901 (\> 0.9) was created. Therefore, the scale exhibited an acceptable overall fit.

For the convergent validity analysis, as shown in Table [4,](#result) the AVE values were greater than 0.5, and the standardized factor loading (λ) of each item ranged from 0.719 to 0.949, above 0.7, suggesting satisfactory convergent validity. With regard to discriminant validity (Table [5)](#in-the-criterion-related-validity-test-of-the-scale-as-shown-in-table6-correlation-analyses-revealed-statistically-signifi--discussion), the square root of AVE for each dimension exceeded its correlations with all other dimensions, indicating good discriminant validity of the instrument.

education. AI not only exists as a tool but also functions as a ubiquitous teacher. Teachers in the field have already rec- ognized this. For instance, research by Kim (2024) indicates that, from teachers’ perspectives, AI needs to maximize the synergy between pedagogy and technology to fulfill subject teaching goals and thereby pave the way for teachers’ effec- tive instruction. This paradigm shift has, to some extent, inverted traditional teaching, steering it toward a more stu- dent-centered approach and personalized learning. Coopera- tion with machine teacher can enhance efficiency and reduce workload for teachers, aiding in the realization of a paradigm shift. Therefore, teachers are supposed to know the capabili- ties of the machine teacher. Building upon the foundation, teachers should apply their pedagogical expertise to address the limitations of AI and even surpass AI. By adopting the proposed model, the study aims to help pinpoint areas where teachers need to improve, enabling them to transition from passive AI receivers to active AI users.

To address research question (2), we analyzed the ques- tionnaire responses. EFL teachers scored above 3.0 in all dimensions of AI-TPACK, indicating their moderate mas- tery of AI-TPACK, including how to use AI and integrate it into their EFL teaching. This aligns with the researchers’ expectations, demonstrating that the professional develop- ment of teachers in the Chinese Smart Education Demon- stration Zone has facilitated the application of AI in EFL teaching. It also indicates that this study has successfully addressed the challenge (2). The AI-TCK score was the high- est, aligning with the previous study (Hava & Babayiğit, [2025)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design) and indicating that teachers have a strong grasp of the knowledge of technology-supported content learning. However, the AI-TPK (machine teacher) score was lowest, possibly due to insufficient pedagogical design in the current AI product (Kim, 2024) and a lack of teacher understanding. In exploring AI-TPACK concerning age, the study revealed that younger teachers exhibited a more profound understand- ing of AI-TCK. This aligns with a previous research about game-related TCK (Hsu et al., [2017)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). It may be attributed to their stage as younger educators, where they are actively engaging in deeper exploration of subject content knowl- edge, and their openness toward technology often tends to a greater number of possibilities. However, the same char- acteristics are not exhibited on other factors, possibly due to the fact that the complexity of integrating AI technol- ogy with pedagogy is far greater than that of integrating AI technology with subject content. Therefore, teachers of all age groups are in the process of learning and adapting. This echoes the highest average score in TCK.

Regarding challenge (3), how can AI-TK be accurately measured, we try to clearly formulate questions to mini- mize ambiguity. In the interviews, it was found that some teachers have difficulty distinguishing AI technology from other technologies (Lindner & Berges, 2020). This study 

X. An et al.

focuses on specific AI technologies in the AI-TK dimen- sion, rather than using the general term “AI technology” as previous study (Ning et al., 2024). Also, the items in this study describe the functions exhibited by AI like “recognize and understand human speech signals,” rather than special- ized technical names like “Natural Language Processing” and “Speech Recognition,” which is different from previous studies (An et al., [2023a)](#on-student-preferences-ai-tpck-ai-tpck-h1-i-know-how-to-human-teacher-use-ai-based-tools-to-design). This is because teachers only need to understand the application level of the technology (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) without needing to know the specific tech- nical terms. By adapting the items in this way, AI-TK can more clearly measure teachers’ knowledge of how to uti- lize AI technologies, preventing teachers from answering the questionnaire based on their vague and misconceived understandings about AI technologies.

## Conclusion and Implication

This study proposed an AI-TPACK model and developed a corresponding instrument specifically tailored for EFL teachers, which demonstrated validity and reliability through the conducted analysis. This instrument can be utilized to assess the AI-TPACK performance of EFL teachers, ena- bling them to self-evaluate their strengths and weaknesses and continuously improve their competencies. Additionally, this tool can assist educational institutions and teacher edu- cators in developing training programs or courses by identi- fying the knowledge areas that need to be addressed.

## Limitation and Future Study

Although this study has proposed a valid and reliable AI- TPACK scale, there are certain limitations to be acknowl- edged. The research sample was collected only from the Chinese Smart Education Demonstration Zone. Therefore, future studies could validate the effectiveness of the scale by incorporating participants from different regions and expand the scope to include a broader population of teachers, such as pre-service and elementary EFL teachers. Additionally, this AI-TPACK framework could be extended to other disci- plines, such as mathematics, with the development of appro- priate measurement tools. Furthermore, it is important to note that the current technology still has imperfections, such as insufficient integration of pedagogical elements. With the ongoing development of technology and its application in practical scenarios, there is potential for the further develop- ment of new TPACK questionnaires.
